lessons.title: Sequences and simple nth terms
lessons.summary: Describe a repeated change, build a pattern and use its position to find a term.
lessons.objective: Describe a repeated change, build a pattern and use its position to find a term.
lessons.before: A sequence is an ordered list. Compare terms side by side to see the repeated change.
lessons.ideas:
Subtract an earlier number from the next. A negative difference tells you the sequence goes down.

If the same count of pieces is added, the totals form a linear sequence.

If the first terms are 5, 6, 7, each is four more than its position. The rule is \(n+4\).
lessons.method:
Check your rule between more than one pair of terms.

Mark the added pieces in a different colour to explain the growth.

Test a suggested rule using both the first and the second positions.
mistakes: The difference is the change, not a new term by itself.
Position 1 belongs to the first whole design. Decide where the count starts.
The value of a term and its position are different quantities.

examples.title: Extending a sequence
examples.question:
The first four terms of a sequence are 5, 3, 1, -1. The same change happens each time.

  1. Find the fifth term.

    [2]

  2. Describe the term-to-term rule.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The change from 5 to 3 is -2.

Apply the same change to the fourth term, -1.

\(-3\).

(b) The difference is -2 at each step.

Subtract 2 each time.

examples.title: Extending a sequence
examples.question:
A row of seats starts with 18 seats. Each new version of the row has 2 more seats. The first four counts are 18, 20, 22, 24.

  1. Find the fifth term.

    [2]

  2. Describe the term-to-term rule.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The change from 18 to 20 is 2.

Apply the same change to the fourth term, 24.

\(26\).

(b) The difference is 2 at each step.

Add 2 each time.

examples.title: A rule for any term
examples.question:
The first four terms are 31, 62, 93, 124. The first term has position 1. The sequence keeps the same difference between terms.

  1. Write the nth term.

    [2]

  2. Find the number in position 2.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Compare positions 1, 2, 3 and 4 with the listed terms.

Each term is 31 times its position.

\(31n\)

(b) Replace n with 2 in \(31n\).

\(62\).

lessons.title: Function machines and linear rules
lessons.summary: Find an output, reverse a rule and use a function to describe a simple situation.
lessons.objective: Find an output, reverse a rule and use a function to describe a simple situation.
lessons.before: A function always gives one output for each allowed input. An instruction such as adding five is one example.
lessons.ideas:
Apply the same rule to each new input. Label the direction from input to output.

Go back through a rule using the inverse operation. Then check using the forward rule.

Adding a constant gives \(y=x+c\). Multiplying by a fixed factor gives \(y=mx\).
lessons.method:
Write the operation before calculating.

Check your input by following the machine forwards again.

Name what x and y represent in the situation.
mistakes: Changing the rule when the input changes makes a different function.
Running the original operation twice usually does not recover the input.
A fixed charge should be added once. A price per item should be multiplied by the number of items.

examples.title: Using a function
examples.question:
A function machine takes an integer input and adds 2. One input is 5.

  1. What is the output for that input?

    [2]

  2. Find the input for output 10.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Apply the rule by adding 2.

\(7\).

(b) Undo adding 2 by subtracting 2.

\(8\).

examples.title: Working backwards through a function
examples.question:
A function machine multiplies its input by 2. One output is 36.

  1. Find its input.

    [2]

  2. Find the output for input 19.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Undo multiplication by 2 by dividing 36 by 2.

\(18\).

(b) Apply the forward rule to 19.

\(38\).

examples.title: Matching a rule to a situation
examples.question:
A bag weighs 4 g when empty. If the contents weigh x g, the full bag weighs y g.

  1. Write a function that links x and y.

    [2]

  2. Find y when x is 2.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Add the bag's fixed weight.

\(y=x+4\)

(b) Use \(y=x+4\) with x = 2.

\(6\).

lessons.title: Plotting straight lines and parallel lines
lessons.summary: Generate coordinates from a rule and recognise horizontal and vertical straight lines.
lessons.objective: Generate coordinates from a rule and recognise horizontal and vertical straight lines.
lessons.before: Choose a few x-values. For each one, substitute into the equation to work out y.
lessons.ideas:
Read every row as an ordered pair \((x,y)\). Plot x along the horizontal axis and y along the vertical axis.

Every point on a horizontal line has the same y-value. Its equation has the form \(y=c\).

Every point on a vertical line has the same x-value. Its equation has the form \(x=c\).
lessons.method:
Make a short table that shows where the coordinates came from.

Think horizontally before naming the fixed coordinate.

Name the coordinate that stays fixed before writing an equation.
mistakes: Swapping the coordinates moves the point to a different place in general.
A line parallel to the x-axis has fixed y, even though its x-values change.
A vertical line through a point does not take its fixed value from that point's second coordinate.

examples.title: Build a table for a line
examples.question:
Draw part of the straight line given by \(y=5x\). The table needs x = 0, 1 and 2.

  1. Find y in the table when x = 2.

    [2]

  2. Complete all three rows, plot them on a grid and draw the line through them.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Replace x by 2.

Multiply by 5.

\(10\).

(b) Use x for the horizontal position and y for the vertical position.

The coordinate pairs are \((0,0), (1,5), (2,10)\). The graph is a straight line through all three.

examples.title: Lines parallel to an axis
examples.question:
A straight line is parallel to the x-axis. It passes through the point \((2,-5)\).

  1. Write the equation of this line.

    [2]

  2. Write the coordinates of another point on the line.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Only the x-coordinate changes along the line.

Every point has y = -5.

\(y=-5\)

(b) Keep y fixed and choose a different x-value.

For example, \((0,-5)\).

examples.title: Lines parallel to an axis
examples.question:
A straight line is parallel to the y-axis. It passes through the point \((8,2)\).

  1. Write the equation of this line.

    [2]

  2. Write the coordinates of another point on the line.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Only the y-coordinate changes along the line.

Every point has x = 8.

\(x=8\)

(b) Keep x fixed and choose a different y-value.

For example, \((8,0)\).

lessons.title: Reading changes on a graph
lessons.summary: Interpret a horizontal part, find a change and compare rates from graph segments.
lessons.objective: Interpret a horizontal part, find a change and compare rates from graph segments.
lessons.before: The horizontal axis still moves forward in time. Read how long a segment lasts by subtracting its start time from its end time.
lessons.ideas:
A flat segment shows that the value on the vertical axis stays the same.

Use the final reading minus the starting reading. If a graph starts above zero, the final height alone gives the wrong change.

Divide the change by the elapsed time. If times match, compare vertical changes directly.
lessons.method:
Use the axis labels to explain the flat part in words.

State the start and end values before finding the change.

Keep track of the units, such as centimetres per minute.
mistakes: A flat segment does not mean that time has stopped. It means the measured value has stopped changing.
Do not confuse the distance from a place with the distance just travelled.
The segment drawn higher up need not have the larger rate.

examples.title: Reading a journey graph
examples.question:
A distance-time graph shows how far a walker has moved away from a shelter, then how long they stop.

Time (minutes)Distance from shelter (m)
00
588
888

  1. How long is the walker stopped?

    [2]

  2. Explain why the final graph segment is horizontal.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The last two distances are both 88 m.

The time from 5 to 8 minutes is 3 minutes.

\(3\) minutes.

(b) The last two readings are at the same height.

Time increases while the distance from the shelter stays constant. In this walk the pupil has stopped.

examples.title: Reading a journey graph
examples.question:
At the start of a recorded route a walker is already 77 m from a shelter. The walker moves farther away, then stops. The first section is a straight line.

Time (minutes)Distance from shelter (m)
077
1882
2182

  1. How far does the distance change during the first 18 minutes?

    [2]

  2. Explain why the final graph segment is horizontal.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Compare the distances at the ends of the first segment.

Subtract 77 m from 82 m.

\(5\) m.

(b) The last two readings are at the same height.

Time increases while the distance from the shelter stays constant. In this walk the pupil has stopped.

examples.title: Comparing slopes with the same time step
examples.question:
A tank fills in two stages. Its depth-time graph has one straight segment for each interval.

Time (minutes)Water depth (cm)
030
258
490

  1. Which interval has the greater rate of increase in water depth?

    [2]

  2. Find the rate of increase over the second interval.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The rises in the same time are 28 cm and 32 cm.

The second rise is larger in the same time, so the second segment is steeper.

\(2\text{ to }4\) minutes

(b) Divide the rise of 32 cm by 2 minutes.

\(16\) cm per minute.
